--- title: "6 Lags & Autocorrelation" --- # 6 Lags & Autocorrelation Time series differ from classical datasets because observations are **not independent**. The value at time t often depends on previous values. We examine this temporal dependence using: - **Lags** - **Autocorrelation** --- ::: {.callout-note title="Note"} Temporal dependence is a core feature of time series. Without it, meaningful forecasting would not be possible. ::: --- ## 6.1 Example Signal ::: {#94fa2cb5 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import pandas as pd import matplotlib.pyplot as plt rng = np.random.default_rng(21) t = pd.date_range("2025-01-01", periods=24*14, freq="H") trend = np.linspace(0, 2, len(t)) season = 0.8 * np.sin(2*np.pi*(t.hour)/24) noise = 0.4 * rng.normal(size=len(t)) s = pd.Series(15 + trend + season + noise, index=t, name="signal") s.plot(title="Example Signal") plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` C:\Users\User\AppData\Local\Temp\ipykernel_14212\4251952496.py:7: FutureWarning: 'H' is deprecated and will be removed in a future version, please use 'h' instead. ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](06-lags-autokorrelation_files/figure-html/cell-2-output-2.png){width=566 height=461} ::: ::: --- ## 6.2 Lag Features A lag shifts the time series backward. ::: {.panel-tabset} ## Pandas ::: {#2887b134 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} lag_1h = s.shift(1) lag_24h = s.shift(24) df_lags = pd.DataFrame({ "y": s, "lag_1h": lag_1h, "lag_24h": lag_24h }) df_lags.head() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ## NumPy (Concept) ::: {#7a5f3e88 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} y = s.to_numpy() lag1 = np.roll(y, 1) lag24 = np.roll(y, 24) lag1[0] = np.nan lag24[:24] = np.nan ``` ::: ::: --- ::: {.callout-tip title="Interpretation"} A high correlation between y(t) and y(t-24) indicates a daily periodicity. ::: --- ## 6.3 Calculating Autocorrelation Autocorrelation measures the correlation between y(t) and y(t-k). ::: {.panel-tabset} ## Pandas ::: {#54fc0375 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} lags = range(1, 49) ac = [s.corr(s.shift(k)) for k in lags] plt.stem(list(lags), ac) plt.title("Autocorrelation (1–48 hours)") plt.xlabel("Lag (h)") plt.ylabel("Correlation") plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](06-lags-autokorrelation_files/figure-html/cell-5-output-1.png){width=594 height=449} ::: ::: ## NumPy (Principle) ::: {#9c28f593 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import matplotlib.pyplot as plt y = s.to_numpy() y = y - np.nanmean(y) def autocorr(y, k): return np.corrcoef(y[:-k], y[k:])[0,1] lags = range(1, 49) ac_np = [autocorr(y, k) for k in lags] plt.stem(list(lags), ac_np) plt.title("Autocorrelation (NumPy)") plt.xlabel("Lag") plt.ylabel("Correlation") plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](06-lags-autokorrelation_files/figure-html/cell-6-output-1.png){width=594 height=449} ::: ::: ::: --- ## 6.4 Interpretation of Autocorrelation Typical patterns: - Slowly decreasing curve → strong trend - Periodic peaks (e.g., at 24, 48, 72) → seasonality - Rapid drop toward 0 → weak dependence --- ::: {.callout-warning title="Warning"} A trend can artificially increase autocorrelation. If necessary, first detrend or difference the series. ::: --- ## 6.5 Mini Exercises 1. Remove the trend (e.g., using a rolling mean). - How does the autocorrelation change? 2. Create a time series without seasonality. - What does the autocorrelation function look like? 3. Generate purely random data. - What do you expect?
